title: California may gut state net neutrality law to comply with Trump admin demand
gist: California is poised to accept $1.86 billion in federal BEAD broadband funds on NTIA terms that bar the state from enforcing net neutrality, rate regulation or 'utility-style rules' against any subgrantee anywhere in the state for up to 14 years. Roughly 69 percent of the money flows to Comcast, AT&T, Verizon/Frontier, Amazon's Kuiper and SpaceX's Starlink, and advocates warn that accepting first forfeits the state's best legal venue — the Ninth Circuit — leaving only a near-unwinnable DC Circuit challenge.

themes.theme: The BEAD conditions and their scope

insights.claim: When the Trump administration overhauled the $42 billion Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment program last year, it ruled that states must agree not to enforce any rate regulation or net neutrality rule on ISPs receiving funding.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A $42 billion program is being used as the lever to achieve deregulation that courts previously blocked.
insights.locator: When the Trump administration overhauled the $42 billion

insights.claim: The NTIA requires participating states to exempt ISPs from net neutrality rules and price regulations in all parts of the state — not merely in areas funded to deploy broadband — with the exemption lasting up to 14 years.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Statewide scope means a small grant buys a carrier regulatory immunity across its entire footprint.
insights.locator: must exempt ISPs from net neutrality rules and price regulations in all parts of the state

insights.claim: The 14-year figure comes from stacking four years for ISPs to deploy the required networks with a 10-year extended period of performance, according to Paul Goodman of the Center for Accessible Technology.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The duration is derived from program mechanics, not a headline number — it outlasts three gubernatorial terms.
insights.locator: Goodman said the exemption from state laws would last for up to 14 years

insights.claim: The NTIA's written rule bars states from enforcing any law that 'directly or indirectly regulates the rates, terms, and conditions of broadband Internet service... or imposes net neutrality rules, open access, or other utility-style rules' against a subgrantee or its affiliates anywhere it provides service in the state.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The words 'or its affiliates' and 'indirectly' make the preemption far broader than net neutrality alone.
insights.quote: imposes net neutrality rules, open access, or other utility-style rules on broadband Internet service, against a Subgrantee or its affiliates anywhere it provides service within the State
insights.locator: The NTIA’s BEAD rules say each state

insights.claim: The NTIA justified statewide scope by arguing that applying net neutrality and rate regulation at non-BEAD locations 'could raise compliance costs and threaten the overall financial viability of the Subgrantee,' increasing default risk at BEAD locations.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The stated rationale treats any state consumer regulation as a solvency threat — a framing that would justify almost unlimited preemption.
insights.quote: could raise compliance costs and threaten the overall financial viability of the Subgrantee
insights.locator: The NTIA said the exemption from state laws must extend statewide

insights.claim: The BEAD law enacted by Congress and President Biden in 2021 requires funded ISPs to offer 'low-cost' plans to low-income people, but the Trump administration told states they cannot set the rates of those plans — so ISPs pick the price of the mandated low-cost offerings themselves.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A low-cost mandate whose price the seller sets is functionally unenforceable — the affordability provision is hollowed out.
insights.locator: The BEAD law enacted by Congress and President Biden in 2021

themes.theme: California's decision point and legal strategy

insights.claim: California and Illinois are the only states that have not finalized their BEAD funding, and the California Public Utilities Commission is scheduled to vote on a resolution ratifying the state's final BEAD plan.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: With 48 states already signed, California is the last realistic venue for a legal challenge to the conditions.
insights.locator: California and Illinois are the only states that haven’t finalized their funding

insights.claim: Paul Goodman called the CPUC vote 'the beginning of the end,' arguing that winning a court battle becomes much harder once the state accepts the money, and urged the CPUC to delay and sue over the legality of the NTIA condition.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Sequencing is the whole game — the legal option expires at the moment of acceptance.
insights.quote: It’s the beginning of the end
insights.locator: Goodman said

insights.claim: Once California accepts the money, its attorney general could only challenge the requirements in the US Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit, which Goodman says 'can really only review that decision for basically fraud or corruption, which is a really high bar to prove.'
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Venue and standard of review, not the merits, will determine whether these conditions are ever tested.
insights.quote: can really only review that decision for basically fraud or corruption, which is a really high bar to prove
insights.locator: Goodman said that once California accepts the money

insights.claim: If California sues before finalizing the agreement, it could bring the case in the Ninth Circuit, which Goodman says has 'a sort of favorable view of that claim,' giving the state a 'pretty good view of success' compared with an 'enormously more difficult' DC Circuit path.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A concrete, time-boxed strategic fork worth tracking: pre-signature Ninth Circuit versus post-signature DC Circuit.
insights.quote: Not impossible, but enormously more difficult
insights.locator: In the DC Circuit, “it’s a much, much harder push,” he said

insights.claim: The CPUC has a deadline at the end of the month to sign the agreement with NTIA but can obtain a 30-day extension and challenge the case in court, per Goodman.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A 30-day extension is the specific procedural window in which litigation must be launched.
insights.locator: He said the CPUC has a deadline at the end of this month

insights.claim: A CPUC spokesperson characterized the vote as a 'procedural requirement' ratifying the December 19, 2025 draft California Final Proposal that NTIA approved on July 17, 2026, and said the resolution 'does not address subgrantee agreements, or the conditions the NTIA requires be included in subgrantee agreements.'
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The state agency and the advocates disagree fundamentally about whether this vote is consequential — that dispute is the story's crux.
insights.quote: The Resolution adopts the now-approved California Final Proposal only. It does not address subgrantee agreements
insights.locator: In a statement to Ars, a CPUC spokesperson said

insights.claim: California is set to receive $1.86 billion in BEAD money and is slated to spend about $1.4 billion deploying broadband to 270,571 locations.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Roughly $5,200 per location deployed — the price at which the state is being asked to trade away 14 years of regulatory authority.
insights.locator: Of the $1.86 billion in BEAD money for the state

insights.claim: Stanford Law professor Barbara van Schewick calculates that roughly 69 percent of California's BEAD funding flows to five large national providers: Comcast ($400 million), AT&T ($331 million), Verizon/Frontier ($173 million), Amazon's Kuiper satellite service ($55 million) and SpaceX's Starlink ($22 million).
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The named beneficiaries and dollar amounts show incumbents capturing most of a program framed as closing the digital divide — and gaining statewide regulatory immunity with it.
insights.quote: Roughly 69 percent of California’s BEAD funding flows to five large, national providers
insights.locator: Stanford Law professor Barbara van Schewick wrote today

insights.claim: The NTIA-mandated state-law exemption applies to any ISP receiving BEAD funds, explicitly including SpaceX's Starlink satellite division.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Satellite entrants gain the same statewide exemption as incumbents for comparatively small grants — $22 million buys Starlink 14 years of immunity.
insights.locator: would also apply to any other ISP receiving BEAD funding

insights.claim: Goodman warns that because the NTIA condition forbids rate regulation and utility-style rules generally, AT&T could tell California it cannot regulate the price of AT&T's copper landline phone service or require AT&T to serve everybody who wants phone service.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The preemption could bleed into legacy telephone obligations, an area where AT&T is already seeking relief in California.
insights.locator: upon receiving BEAD money, AT&T could tell California

insights.claim: Goodman says BEAD money could jeopardize a merger condition requiring Verizon to offer $20-per-month broadband to low-income Californians, and that the savings from those required plans would dwarf the BEAD money the state is due to receive.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: If true, the state is trading away more consumer value than the grant delivers — a direct net-negative argument.
insights.locator: Goodman said the BEAD money could also jeopardize a merger condition

insights.claim: Van Schewick identifies another casualty: a 2019 California law prohibiting mobile providers from throttling first responders during emergencies, passed after Verizon throttled an 'unlimited' data plan used by Santa Clara County firefighters during a wildfire.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A concrete public-safety protection with a documented triggering incident is inside the scope of the waiver.
insights.quote: left to their own devices, Internet providers have put profits over public safety before. California is now being asked to sign away those protections for fourteen years
insights.locator: “Those protections exist for a reason”

insights.claim: California Assemblymember Tasha Boerner dropped a proposed bill requiring ISPs to offer $15 broadband plans to low-income people after Trump administration officials warned that setting rates would jeopardize the state's access to broadband grants.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Evidence the conditions are already chilling state legislation before any money has been signed for.
insights.locator: California Assemblymember Tasha Boerner proposed a bill

insights.claim: Van Schewick argues California would have a good case because the federal BEAD statute says funded providers must follow state and local laws, contending that 'a federal agency can't use fine print in a grant to override what Congress wrote into the statute.'
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The statutory-text argument is the strongest legal hook and the reason advocates want litigation before signature.
insights.quote: A federal agency can’t use fine print in a grant to override what Congress wrote into the statute
insights.locator: van Schewick wrote

insights.claim: Nearly 30 advocacy groups wrote to Governor Gavin Newsom, Attorney General Rob Bonta and CPUC President John Reynolds warning that accepting the terms 'would set a dangerous precedent for the federal government to use federal funding as a cudgel that forces states in line with its agenda.'
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The coercion-precedent argument extends far beyond broadband to any federal grant program.
insights.quote: would set a dangerous precedent for the federal government to use federal funding as a cudgel that forces states in line with its agenda
insights.locator: The letter to state leaders said

insights.claim: The first Trump administration lost its attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws in court, and the second is pursuing the same result indirectly by making federal broadband money conditional on non-enforcement.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Funding conditions as a substitute for failed preemption litigation is a replicable template across policy areas.
insights.locator: While the first Trump administration lost its attempt to preempt

insights.claim: California's law, which the state defended through a yearslong court battle, prohibits ISPs from blocking or throttling lawful traffic and bars them from charging websites or online services fees to deliver or prioritize traffic to users.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The substance of what would be suspended: both blocking/throttling bans and paid-prioritization bans.
insights.locator: California’s law prohibits ISPs from blocking or throttling lawful traffic

themes.theme: New York as the leading indicator

insights.claim: New York won a court battle less than two years ago defending its Affordable Broadband Act — requiring ISPs to offer $15 or $20 per month service to low-income people — against broadband industry lobby groups, but has agreed to take $664.6 million of BEAD money and may now be unable to enforce the law against grant recipients.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: New York shows the endgame: a hard-won courtroom victory neutralized by accepting federal money.
insights.locator: On the other side of the country, New York may have to stop enforcing

insights.claim: Governor Kathy Hochul said in April 2026 that closing the digital divide requires both universal broadband and ensuring 'that it remains affordable when it gets there,' citing the Affordable Broadband Act and a commitment to reaching the final 1 percent of unserved households.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The stated policy goal now sits in direct tension with the funding terms New York accepted.
insights.quote: that it remains affordable when it gets there
insights.locator: New York Governor Kathy Hochul said in an April 2026 press release
